summary: This informational document discusses why traffic is often spread unevenly over the parallel links in Link Aggregation Groups (LAG) and Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) setups. It surveys mechanisms for using those component links more evenly, so bandwidth is not wasted as traffic demands grow.

eli5.summary: If several checkout lines are open but everyone queues in one, the others sit idle. This note looks at ways to spread network traffic across all the lines evenly.

questions: how to balance traffic across lag links
why does hash based load balancing fail
subtitle: Distributing traffic more fairly across parallel network links

tldr.problem: Networks use parallel links (Link Aggregation Groups and Equal-Cost Multipath) for capacity scaling, but hash-based load balancing distributes traffic unevenly when traffic includes large long-lived flows, leaving some links underutilized while others congest.
tldr.mechanism: Identify large flows (significant bandwidth users lasting seconds or longer), recognize when they cause imbalance, and move them to lightly loaded links or adjust the hash table to exclude congested links from smaller flows.
tldr.outcome: Better link utilization, fewer bottlenecks, and more predictable network performance under heavy or uneven traffic patterns.

facts.value: Many-to-one mapping of flows to links

today: RFC 7424 is an Informational RFC published in January 2015. It describes mechanisms that are implemented in modern switching equipment for traffic engineering and load balancing, particularly in data center and service provider networks. The RFC has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Parallel Links Underperform
sections.content:
Modern networks bundle multiple links together to increase capacity. Link Aggregation Groups (LAGs) bundle physical links between adjacent routers; Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) spreads traffic across multiple paths in a network.

Most routers use hash-based load balancing to decide which link each flow uses: they compute a hash of the flow's identifying fields (source address, destination address, port numbers) to select a component link. This is simple, stateless, and preserves packet order within a flow.

However, hash-based techniques fail when traffic is uneven. If a few large flows happen to hash to the same component link, that link congests while others remain underutilized. A single 50-Gbps backup flow hashing to one link in a four-link LAG could saturate that link, while the others sit nearly idle.
sections.eli5: The router uses a simple math trick to pick which link each flow uses. But if several big flows do the math and land on the same link, that link gets jammed while others have empty space.

sections.title: Understanding Flow Types
sections.content:
This RFC categorizes flows into four types based on bandwidth and duration:

Long-lived large flows (LLLF) are the key problem. These are connections that last for minutes or hours and consume significant bandwidth—such as database replication, backup traffic, or IPsec tunnels. They are called "large flows" in the RFC.

Large flows matter because a few of them can saturate a link. On a 10-Gbps link, a single 2-Gbps flow is significant. Long-lived means the flow stays long enough for operators to react. In contrast, short-lived large flows (a burst for milliseconds) appear and vanish before rebalancing can help, so they are grouped with small flows as "small flows" for optimization purposes.

Large flows consume predictable bandwidth for seconds to hours. This duration is long enough to measure, detect, and move to another link before the flow ends.
sections.eli5: Some network flows are big and long. Others are small or quick. The RFC focuses on big long ones because those are the ones that can jam links, and operators have time to move them.

sections.title: Detecting and Identifying Large Flows
sections.content:
The RFC describes two main approaches to detect large flows.

Sampling techniques (sFlow, PSAMP, NetFlow): Routers sample a fraction of traffic and send samples to a collector. The collector accumulates data and estimates bandwidth per flow. Sampling is supported in most existing equipment and uses minimal CPU. However, sampling introduces a detection delay on high-speed links (collecting enough samples to recognize a 10-Gbps flow takes a second or more) and sampling can miss short-duration spikes.

Inline data path measurement: Some routers can examine every packet passing through them and update counters in real time. This allows detecting large flows in shorter time windows (milliseconds to sub-seconds on high-speed links) and is more accurate. However, this approach requires more memory and router resources to track all flows.

Operators configure two programmable parameters: a bandwidth threshold (e.g., 10% of link capacity) and an observation interval (e.g., 1 second). Any flow exceeding the threshold over the interval is marked as large.
sections.eli5: The router watches traffic and spots big flows. It can count all packets (slow but accurate) or spot-check samples (faster but uses estimates).

sections.title: Rebalancing Traffic
sections.content:
Once large flows are detected, routers can rebalance in two main ways.

Move large flows: The router identifies which component link is congested and which ones are lightly loaded. It then uses policy-based routing rules to move some large flows from the congested link to lighter links. For example, if a 4-Gbps flow on link 1 is causing congestion when link 2 is nearly idle, move that flow to link 2. This minimizes the number of flows affected and their packet reordering.

Exclude congested links from hash table: Alternatively, the router adjusts the hash-based lookup table so that small flows avoid the congested link. The router reduces the "weight" of congested links in the hash function so fewer flows hash to them. Large flows are still explicitly placed, while small flows are hashed into the remaining links.

Neither approach is perfect. Perfect rebalancing is impossible because flows arrive and depart asynchronously. Moving a large flow may momentarily reorder its packets. New flows may appear and require rearrangement. However, these approaches significantly improve utilization compared to doing nothing.
sections.eli5: When a link gets full, the router can move big flows off it or tell small flows to use other links instead.

sections.title: Limitations and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanisms in this RFC are local optimizations, meaning each router makes decisions based only on its own view. This approach works well for LAGs (optimization between adjacent routers has no downstream impact), but for ECMP (which affects paths through multiple hops), local optimization can create bottlenecks downstream that the local router cannot see.

A central management entity with visibility across the network could optimize globally: if router R1 identifies a congested downstream path, a central system might direct flows away from it. The RFC discusses this possibility but notes that many networks lack such visibility, especially across operator boundaries.

Other practical considerations include monitoring frequency (how often to scan for congestion), handling route changes (rebalancing when the ECMP topology shifts), and reserving component links for protection (keeping backup links for failure recovery).

The RFC emphasizes that these mechanisms are complementary to, not a replacement for, IPv6's elimination of address sharing and the associated scaling challenges.
sections.eli5: Each router can optimize its own links, but networks that can see the whole picture might balance better. Routers must keep checking for problems, handle link failures, and be ready to change plans when routes change.
